title: Heat Flux Density: W/m², BTU/(h·ft²) and Solar Constant
h1: Heat flux density — W/m² and BTU/(h·ft²)
description: Solar constant: 1361 W/m² = 431 BTU/(h·ft²). Comfortable radiant panel: 200 W/m². Combustion flame: >100 kW/m². Scales matter.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: W/m² is the SI. HVAC keeps BTU/(h·ft²). Solar, radiant heating and process both live on the same axis.
body: Heat flux density measures how fast energy crosses a surface per unit area. It appears in insulation ratings, solar power, radiant heaters and combustion analysis.

> 1 W/m² = 0.3170 BTU/(h·ft²)
> 1 BTU/(h·ft²) = 3.1546 W/m²
> 1 kW/m² = 316.9 BTU/(h·ft²)

Solar (top of atmosphere): 1361 W/m². Solar at surface (clear noon): 1000 W/m². Human body: 100 W/m². Radiant floor heater: 100–200 W/m². Standard incandescent lamp bulb surface: 30 kW/m². Metal welding arc: 10 000 kW/m².

A 20 m² array at 1000 W/m² intercepts 20 kW of raw solar flux. At 20% panel efficiency, DC output is 4 kW. Skip the flux density unit and confuse it with total incident W — you get 1000 W total (not per m²) and predict a 200 W array output, 20× too low.
W/m² is the currency of radiation and heat transfer. Multiply by 0.317 for BTU/(h·ft²).

faqs.q: Is 'irradiance' the same as heat flux?
faqs.a: Same units, different context — irradiance is specifically for radiation (usually solar or thermal); heat flux includes all mechanisms.

faqs.q: How does emissivity affect heat flux?
faqs.a: Radiative flux is proportional to ε × σ × T⁴. Emissivity ε < 1 reduces flux at a given temperature.
